note: Plain-language glosses for the working surface, agent-written from CAPABILITIES.md and the linked specs. The card and spec win where they disagree; flag a wrong gloss on the surface.

ALTAR-01.title: Banked life charge: sacrifices die, recipients live
ALTAR-01.summary: The altar stores sacrificed blood and life as charge that never decays, so a sacrifice can be banked and spent eras later. A prisoner or slave put in is fuel and dies; anyone else is a recipient and walks out alive.

ALTAR-02.title: Willing believers can give their own lives
ALTAR-02.summary: A colonist can offer their own life at the altar, counted differently from a coerced prisoner, but only if their faith certainty is high enough (e.g. 85%). Nothing re-checks certainty once the rite has started.

ALTAR-03.title: Powered facilities make altar rites cheaper
ALTAR-03.summary: Linking powered facilities to the altar cuts each rite's charge cost, but never below a quarter: technology improves the apparatus, it never replaces the life. For the lottery they will also lean the draw and widen the offer.

ALTAR-04.title: A named gene capsule grants that gene
ALTAR-04.summary: Load a capsule (vector) naming a specific gene and run the rite: the recipient survives with exactly that gene, no gamble. This is how named altar rites keep their promise.

ALTAR-05.title: The altar's gene lottery
ALTAR-05.summary: An opt-in gamble: a roll picks a quality tier, four genes are drawn and offered, and the player must take one. Walking away is no exit; a deadline picks at random. The bad tier lacks teeth until it holds more genes.

ALTAR-06.title: Lottery shows its category, hides its odds
ALTAR-06.summary: Before gambling, the player sees the capsule's gene category and, once drawn, all four genes on offer, but not the probabilities behind them. The alternative publishes odds per option.

ALTAR-07.title: The final rite makes a founder transcendent
ALTAR-07.summary: Once a founder has claimed a self-authored title, the altar's final rite grants the Transcendent gene and leads straight to the Administrator. A transcended founder can never be burned as fuel.

REVERENCE-01.title: Reverence: how far your faith has spread
REVERENCE-01.summary: Each NPC faction has a Reverence number measuring how deeply the player faith has reached its people. It rises when converted visitors or released believer-prisoners go home, and when deeds are credited to the founders.

REVERENCE-02.title: Reverence fades when neglected, announces its bands
REVERENCE-02.summary: Left alone, a faction's Reverence slowly decays; institutions there slow the decay. Crossing a named band threshold, up or down, sends the player a letter.

REVERENCE-03.title: Seeing Reverence and what it will unlock
REVERENCE-03.summary: Reverence is displayed alongside Goodwill, and diplomatic options it will open appear greyed out with their threshold ("requires N Reverence, currently M"), so the player sees the carrot before reaching it.

REVERENCE-04.title: Reverence changes how governments take goodwill
REVERENCE-04.summary: A government with low Goodwill but high Reverence is wary: goodwill gains shrink and losses deepen. At top Reverence it is won over: gains accelerate sharply, losses soften. Factions that cannot hold Reverence, like the Church, are exempt.

REVERENCE-05.title: Churches planted inside friendly factions
REVERENCE-05.summary: With enough Reverence, the player spends Goodwill to found a church or monastery in a friendly faction. It holds Reverence up against decay, is suppressed with a letter if the faction turns hostile, and returns on peace.

CHURCH-01.title: The Empire becomes the Church
CHURCH-01.summary: Royalty's Empire is reskinned in place as a Catholic-like Church: Church quests pay Exaltation (royal favour), and each new title arrives by a ceremony. Nothing is renamed underneath, or everything relying on the Empire breaks.

CHURCH-02.title: Church titles unlock privileges and trade
CHURCH-02.summary: Titles unlock permits, presented as Church privileges, and access to Church traders: Knight to trade, Baron for orbital trade. Trade closes while the Church is hostile.

CHURCH-03.title: Choosing who gets credit for a deed
CHURCH-03.summary: When accepting a public deed, the player picks who is credited: the Church (Exaltation), the founders (Reverence), the Schism once allied (Influence), or a mix, each with its own consequences. Options are fixed when the quest appears.

CHURCH-04.title: Church decrees with real costs for failure
CHURCH-04.summary: Titled colonists receive decrees; failing one costs mood, Exaltation or Goodwill with the Church, set per decree. No decrees arrive while the Church is hostile, and running ones end when it turns hostile.

CHURCH-05.title: Who may hold Church titles
CHURCH-05.summary: Decides whether any colonist can earn Church favour and titles, only the founders, or some other group. One point of favour already makes a title, and a dead holder's favour passes to an heir, so founders-only takes code.

CHURCH-06.title: Betraying the Church is permanent
CHURCH-06.summary: An authored act of betrayal makes the Church hostile forever; gifts and peace talks cannot undo it. Decrees and perks end, titles stay. What triggers the betrayal mission is handled outside this card.

CHURCH-07.title: The Church's ending: sanctioned apotheosis
CHURCH-07.summary: While a founder holds the top Church title, the Church keeps offering apotheosis; accepting ends the campaign for both players. The offer closes for good at betrayal or at the orbital reveal.

FOUNDERS-01.title: Faith roles that unlock over the campaign
FOUNDERS-01.summary: The player faith has seats (founders, preachers, crafting and other specialists) that become available as the campaign reaches milestones, rather than all at once.

FOUNDERS-02.title: The faith's fixed core beliefs
FOUNDERS-02.summary: The campaign lays a base under the player's faith: some precepts are forced, and some have a minimum the player can make stricter but never looser, e.g. tolerance of other faiths. The player authors everything else.

FOUNDERS-03.title: Founders: recognised, required, never given away
FOUNDERS-03.summary: The game knows which two pawns are the founders from day one, lets a beat require them before the player accepts, and refuses every way a founder could be lent, sold, banished to die or kidnapped.

SCHISM-01.title: NPC factions changing their faith
SCHISM-01.summary: An NPC faction's faith can change mid-campaign: about 40% of factions take the Church's faith at Medieval, the Schism turns, or a revolt converts a people. The choice is whether the people themselves convert.

SCHISM-02.title: Revolts that overthrow hostile governments
SCHISM-02.summary: Where a people reveres the player faith but its government is hostile, the player can help them revolt. It can be offered or started, fought or bought, and end anywhere from a faith change to an ally; never a new faction.

SCHISM-03.title: The Schism replaces the Church
SCHISM-03.summary: A hidden rival faction, the Schism, is revealed when the players commit to it, takes Church settlements one plot beat at a time, and becomes a permanent ally. Whatever does not convert stays behind as a hostile Church remnant.

PSYCHIC-01.title: Psylink ranks come from altar rites
PSYCHIC-01.summary: Psychic rank is granted by a rite at the altar, one level at a time, with the first psylink arriving in the Medieval era. The rite can require the giver's faith and certainty.

PSYCHIC-02.title: Meditation does not raise psychic rank
PSYCHIC-02.summary: Under Vanilla Psycasts Expanded, meditation and every psyfocus gain earn XP that raises psylink rank, bypassing the altar. This closes or limits that loop so rank stays the altar's gift.

PSYCHIC-03.title: Closing every other source of psylinks
PSYCHIC-03.summary: Neuroformers, anima trees, the blinding ritual, title ceremonies and some XP abilities all hand out psylink levels. Each is shut so rank comes only from the altar.

PSYCHIC-04.title: Captured casters keep or lose their powers
PSYCHIC-04.summary: Decides whether an enemy psycaster the player captures or recruits keeps their psylink rank. With nothing built, they keep it.

PSYCHIC-05.title: Psycaster paths only founders may enter
PSYCHIC-05.summary: Some Vanilla Psycasts Expanded paths are open only to the two founders, keeping them above their disciples. Any key works, but psytrainers and psyrings slip past it until the path is sealed.

PSYCHIC-06.title: Church psychics capped below the founders
PSYCHIC-06.summary: The Church fields its own psycasters, but their levels are fixed at generation and never climb to the founders' level, whatever titles they hold.

PSYCHIC-07.title: Named psychic ranks
PSYCHIC-07.summary: Psylink levels carry names such as "Adept" instead of just numbers. Plain data can only put the name in a tooltip; showing it on the psylink row or beside the pawn's name takes code.

TRANSCENDENCE-01.title: Each founder's saved transcendence record
TRANSCENDENCE-01.summary: Each founder carries one hidden saved record that every transcendence beat reads: the claimed title, whether it is claimed, when they transcended, and whether they have met the Administrator.

TRANSCENDENCE-02.title: Claim Yourself: the founder's self-written title
TRANSCENDENCE-02.summary: The player types a self-authored title for a founder. Until they do, the altar refuses the final rite with "X has not claimed a title".

TRANSCENDENCE-03.title: The claimed title shown in play
TRANSCENDENCE-03.summary: The founder's self-chosen title appears in the game, by default in the inspect pane, Bio tab and generated text as "Name, Title". Showing it on the colonist bar and map label needs extra work.

TRANSCENDENCE-04.title: Meeting the Administrator: Enter or Stay
TRANSCENDENCE-04.summary: After the final rite each founder meets the Administrator once and chooses to Enter the new reality or Stay. Stay changes nothing; the founder remains transcendent and in play.

TRANSCENDENCE-05.title: Entering the new reality: credits or game over
TRANSCENDENCE-05.summary: Choosing Enter rolls credits, ends the game, or both. Credits alone leave the second founder's arc open; ending the game closes the playthrough for both players.

POLITICS-01.title: Wronging one faction angers its allies too
POLITICS-01.summary: Kidnapping, harming, killing or stripping a faction's people, or fouling ground near its settlement, also costs goodwill with that faction's allies, each announced by letter. Works only on alliances the campaign seeds at game start; NPC factions start with none.

POLITICS-02.title: Faction demands with a deadline and stated consequence
POLITICS-02.summary: A faction asks for something specific, with a countdown, and the letter states what happens either way before the player answers. Serving it can cost goodwill with its rival, named in a message.

POLITICS-03.title: What demands can ask the colony for
POLITICS-03.summary: Demands aim at what the colony can actually do: silver, goods to a tile, a colonist on loan, a skilled specialist, an embargo on a rival, a bandit camp cleared, refugees hosted, an escort, a prisoner freed. Each detects success and failure.

POLITICS-04.title: Refusing a demand has a real price
POLITICS-04.summary: The player refuses by letting the offer expire. The consequence the letter promised then fires, such as lost goodwill or a retaliation raid, and refusing can win standing with the refused faction's enemies.

POLITICS-05.title: Rival factions' opposing demands in one letter
POLITICS-05.summary: Two rivals want opposite things in a single quest. The player sees both branches with their prices, e.g. 'serve the Reach: +Reach, −Clans', and picking one fails the other.

POLITICS-06.title: A cap on simultaneous diplomatic demands
POLITICS-06.summary: Keeps the number of live demands manageable so the players aren't buried in letters: new demand offers stop once a set number are pending.

POLITICS-07.title: Locked rewards that show the standing needed
POLITICS-07.summary: Standing with a faction unlocks things, and locked ones are visible early with their price: 'need 60 Reverence with the Reach (now 42)'. The gate can read Goodwill, Reverence or Exaltation.

POLITICS-08.title: Who hates whom stays secret until earned
POLITICS-08.summary: Vanilla shows every faction's enemies on the Factions tab. Here that is withheld until standing, a quest, a comms question or a battle reveals it, faction by faction, and a locked row says what earns it. Alliances can be shown too.

POLITICS-09.title: Caravans meet the settlements they pass
POLITICS-09.summary: A caravan travelling near a settlement meets its faction: a hostile one ambushes or demands a toll, a friendly one offers trade. Makes world-map travel political.

POLITICS-10.title: Ways out of a losing war
POLITICS-10.summary: A war the colony is losing can end: gifts and peace talks, terms the colony proposes, a one-off reparation, or becoming a tributary with scheduled payments and obligations. Works against any faction whose goodwill can change.

POLITICS-11.title: Easing a war with the Glitterites or Archons
POLITICS-11.summary: The Glitterites and Archons are permanent enemies by design, outside diplomacy. A war with them can be eased, fewer raids for a price, but not ended unless the campaign deliberately lifts their permanent-enemy status.

TERRITORY-01.title: Joining an ally's battle, or hearing who won
TERRITORY-01.summary: An ally under attack calls for help at a tile with a short window. Go and it's a real three-way fight; stay home and it resolves without the colony, with the outcome reported by letter.

TERRITORY-02.title: What an outpost costs and pays back
TERRITORY-02.summary: Founding an outpost costs materials, silver and the colonists sent to run it, and its yield must make that worthwhile. Built on Vanilla Expanded's outposts, which as shipped cost nothing to found.

TERRITORY-03.title: Colonists sent to an outpost are gone
TERRITORY-03.summary: The pawns committed to an outpost leave the colony for good, and the outpost runs itself with nothing to manage. A build can require or forbid a kind of pawn, such as needing one free colonist.

TERRITORY-04.title: Outposts get attacked; fallen ones become ruins
TERRITORY-04.summary: Outposts cost attention through events, not management screens. The required event is an attack: defend it or it's destroyed into a ruin whose goods can be looted and which can be rebuilt for a price.

TERRITORY-05.title: Conquering a settlement is a real siege
TERRITORY-05.summary: Taking an NPC settlement means real walls, turrets or siege engines and real defenders, harder at higher tech tiers. Vanilla bases are soft, and have no turrets or mortars before the Industrial era.

TERRITORY-06.title: Conquered settlements become tribute-paying holdings
TERRITORY-06.summary: A settlement the colony takes becomes its holding: it owes the colony goods but is never a map the player runs. The engine has no vassal relation, so this must be built.

TERRITORY-07.title: What a holding pays, and how it arrives
TERRITORY-07.summary: A new holding first owes a rebuild debt. After that it pays what it's known for, e.g. slaves from a slaver tribe or arms from an armourer, on a schedule, delivered wherever home is, even the gravship.

TERRITORY-08.title: Learning what a settlement is known for
TERRITORY-08.summary: Each faction has a public specialty and each settlement its own, made plausible by its tile. A settlement's specialty is learned only by going there: visiting, trading, passing nearby or scouting.

TERRITORY-09.title: Showing what's learned, hiding what vanilla leaks
TERRITORY-09.summary: A learned specialty shows on hover, in a tab, in world search and in the attack menu. Before that, vanilla's leaks are closed: the sellable-items window, tier hints in faction names and art, and the Empire's trade-permit line.

TERRITORY-10.title: Paying to advance a holding one era
TERRITORY-10.summary: A holding stays at the era it was taken until the colony pays to advance it one era, never beyond the colony's own. The era advance itself never upgrades holdings for free.

TERRITORY-11.title: How a holding is lost or given up
TERRITORY-11.summary: A holding ends by release, retaking, destruction or revolt, always as a moment the player can act on, never a hidden roll. The place passes to a randomly drawn faction, and whatever it still owed is cancelled.

TERRITORY-12.title: Settlements never change hands under the players
TERRITORY-12.summary: When a settlement changes owner, at the era advance, the Schism or a conquest, it never happens while players are on its map, and caravans heading there are dealt with. A parked gravship is the one unsolved case.

TERRITORY-13.title: Sworn factions provide services, asked or offered
TERRITORY-13.summary: A faction sworn to the colony owes help, not goods: troops, lent specialists, traders, a shuttle. The player can ask for services as well as receive them on the faction's own schedule; higher Reverence opens more.

PRESSURE-01.title: How strong raids get, and from what
PRESSURE-01.summary: Raid strength comes from capped inputs: time spent in the current era, military strength, Reverence and enemy count, with wealth only a minor share.

PRESSURE-02.title: How often threats come, set apart from size
PRESSURE-02.summary: Threat frequency follows campaign state, enemy count and time in the era, independently of raid size, so threats can become more frequent without each one getting bigger, or the reverse.

PRESSURE-03.title: Fewer, tougher enemies instead of hordes
PRESSURE-03.summary: Late threats stay dangerous through quality, not just numbers: 'four juggernauts, not forty men'. Stronger raids can also unlock an era's signature raid rather than more bodies.

PRESSURE-04.title: More enemy factions mean more pressure
PRESSURE-04.summary: Each hostile faction adds to threat size and frequency, and alliances count too, so diplomacy changes how hard the colony is pressed.

PRESSURE-05.title: Authored raids with a fixed faction and size
PRESSURE-05.summary: A story beat, a refused demand or the Glitterite pursuit can send a raid with a set faction, strength and tactic, instead of whatever the storyteller would roll.

PRESSURE-06.title: Reverence also brings friendly arrivals
PRESSURE-06.summary: As Reverence rises, the colony draws welcome arrivals alongside bigger threats: pilgrims, offerings, volunteers. The positive half of the storyteller.

PRESSURE-07.title: Story beats protected from random chance
PRESSURE-07.summary: The campaign's ordered story beats fire reliably and aren't pre-empted or swamped by random storyteller events. Four vanilla levers, all data only.

PRESSURE-08.title: Raids that come for something specific
PRESSURE-08.summary: A raid can declare its aim, people, livestock or stores, named in its letter ('Slave raid: the Ashen Clans'), and leaves once it has it. The player reads the aim before the group arrives.

PRESSURE-09.title: Hated factions come harder and more often
PRESSURE-09.summary: A faction that truly hates the colony raids more often, in greater strength, and with nastier tactics than one that merely dislikes it. Goodwill bottoms out at −100, so hatred is built on top of it.

PRESSURE-10.title: Players can see what's raising pressure
PRESSURE-10.summary: A readout tells the players broadly what is driving threats up, so pressure feels explicable rather than arbitrary.

ENCOUNTERS-01.title: A told encounter arrives on its own timer
ENCOUNTERS-01.summary: An optional told encounter, such as the anima-teaching visit, is offered on its own schedule: a fixed day, a day drawn from a range, 'maybe' after a day, or again after it lapses.

ENCOUNTERS-02.title: Offered by a randomly drawn friendly faction
ENCOUNTERS-02.summary: The encounter comes from a faction drawn at random among those not hostile to the colony, so who tells the story varies from game to game.

ENCOUNTERS-03.title: Encounter held at a site the colony visits
ENCOUNTERS-03.summary: The colony caravans to the giver's site, such as a village by an anima tree, and receives the teaching there, with a passage on arrival.

ENCOUNTERS-04.title: Visitors come to venerate the colony's anima tree
ENCOUNTERS-04.summary: Instead of the colony travelling, the giver's people come to it, walk to its anima tree, venerate it and leave. Harming the tree or the visitors ends the rite.

ENCOUNTERS-05.title: The encounter teaches without granting power
ENCOUNTERS-05.summary: What the encounter delivers is knowledge, not power: a passage, a memory, a mark, a techprint for research reachable anyway, or a fact later content can check.

ENCOUNTERS-06.title: Ignoring the encounter costs nothing
ENCOUNTERS-06.summary: The encounter is always optional: ignoring it has no penalty, an unvisited site cleans itself up, and it never grants a psylink.

TRACE-01.title: How much the Glitterites know about you
TRACE-01.summary: A single 0–100 Trace score split into low, rising and high bands. Entering a band switches its effects on, such as blocked incidents or more Glitterite raids, so the threat escalates with the founders' exposure.

TRACE-02.title: What raises and lowers Trace
TRACE-02.summary: Deep hacks (more if detected), missions against the Glitterites and analysing their artifacts raise Trace; a basic local hack like a door costs nothing. Glitterite quests can lower it, and it fades a little each day.

TRACE-03.title: Trace brings more Glitterite raids, not bigger
TRACE-03.summary: Higher bands make the Glitterites a likelier raider and switch certain incidents on or off. Ordinary raids never grow with Trace, so it cannot stack with Reverence's pressure; only pursuit raids scale.

TRACE-04.title: The hidden hunt and its countdown
TRACE-04.summary: A separate search runs unseen, faster at higher Trace. Past a reveal point a countdown appears in the quest tab, and it shortens or lengthens the instant Trace changes.

TRACE-05.title: Found: a huge raid, then raids until escape
TRACE-05.summary: When the search completes, a large detection raid hits, scaled by difficulty and Trace. Raids then repeat on an authored on/off cycle until the colony escapes; staying to fight forever is allowed.

TRACE-06.title: Moving far enough shakes off the hunt
TRACE-06.summary: Relocating the colony a long way (gravship, or caravan out, found a new base, abandon the old) resets the search to zero. Trace itself stays. A short hop resets nothing, so it buys no fresh safe window.

TRACE-07.title: Leaving the planet always escapes
TRACE-07.summary: A jump between the surface and orbit, either direction, always counts as a full escape. A move between two places in orbit is judged against its own escape distance, since orbit tiles differ from planet tiles.

TRACE-08.title: The hunt when there are two colonies
TRACE-08.summary: With two colonies, the pursuit can hunt each separately, only one (the other a permanent haven), or the founders' people wherever they are. Every version must name which settlement counts as a colony.

TRACE-09.title: Showing Trace to the player
TRACE-09.summary: The player sees the current band and its effects, what a mission does to Trace before accepting, a letter when the band changes, the pursuit countdown once revealed, and a Trace number always on screen.

CURRENCIES-01.title: Influence and Intel as banked currencies
CURRENCIES-01.summary: Two saved balances, Influence and Intel, always visible on screen. Missions, artifact analysis and site lore pay into them; they are spent on the Schism, favours, bought missions and Instruction items.

CURRENCIES-02.title: Is Intel a number or an item?
CURRENCIES-02.summary: Intel can be an abstract balance or a physical stockpiled item. A number can be earned by reading lore but needs its own display; an item shows in the resource list for free but can never come from lore.

CURRENCIES-03.title: Missions that pay Influence or Intel
CURRENCIES-03.summary: A mission can list Influence or Intel as a reward, visible before accepting, and can offer different currencies as alternative rewards or per approach, so the player chooses what the deed earns.

CURRENCIES-04.title: Earning Intel from artifacts and site lore
CURRENCIES-04.summary: Intel also comes from slowly dismantling Glitterite artifacts and, optionally, from investigating lore at sites, so curiosity is rewarded with something useful rather than loot.

CURRENCIES-05.title: Trading Intel for techprints
CURRENCIES-05.summary: The player spends Intel to buy Instruction: techprints or authored items that unlock research. Besides the quest shop, it is the only thing that spends Intel.

CURRENCIES-06.title: Buying missions with currency
CURRENCIES-06.summary: A shop where the player spends Influence or Intel to buy a specific mission, which then starts. This is how the campaign's purchasable missions reach the player.

CURRENCIES-07.title: What the shop sells, and when
CURRENCIES-07.summary: Each shop entry is a mission or an item, with its own unlock condition (research, era, a balance or a political flag) and its own clock for leaving the shelf or restocking.

CURRENCIES-08.title: A failed bought mission comes back
CURRENCIES-08.summary: If a paid-for mission fails, it can return to the shop free, at its price, refunded, after a delay or capped, set per entry. It always returns as a fresh roll, never the same mission.

CURRENCIES-09.title: Spending Influence to advance the Schism
CURRENCIES-09.summary: The Schism plot is an ordered chain of paid blows: spend Influence to launch the next; success moves on, failure re-offers it. A marking act commits the founders and turns the Church permanently hostile.

CURRENCIES-10.title: Currencies that decay or expire
CURRENCIES-10.summary: Influence or Intel could shrink over time, which decides whether hoarding pays. It is possible either way and not yet chosen; decay below a Schism step's price could stall the plot.

HACKING-01.title: Tougher security guards better targets
HACKING-01.summary: Hackable targets carry security (ICE) tiered by value, with two new top tiers for Glitterite and Archon systems. A valuable target always gets its hardest tier rather than a random one.

HACKING-02.title: Research opens new kinds of hack target
HACKING-02.summary: Research unlocks what can be hacked, in order: defences, then reactors, then weaker mechs, then strong mechs. A locked target refuses the hack and says why.

HACKING-03.title: Glitterite trophies unlock advanced hacking
HACKING-03.summary: Top-tier hacking research requires having studied specific Glitterite objects the colony brought home and, where authored, an Instruction item bought with Intel.

HACKING-04.title: A steady supply of new hacking abilities
HACKING-04.summary: Hacking keeps gaining verbs over the campaign, from bypassing a door to seizing mechs and turning defences. Abilities are learned from data taken in hacks, never bought.

HACKING-05.title: Hijack turrets and mechs, trigger remote effects
HACKING-05.summary: A hack can flip an enemy turret onto its owners or disable and then hijack a mech, so a mission need not kill every defender. A hack at one console can also cause an effect elsewhere.

HACKING-06.title: Hacking remotely through a field agent
HACKING-06.summary: A skilled hacker stays home sealed in a Cyberpod while a colonist at an away site carries a relay; the hack uses the home hacker's skill. The field colonist must still stand at the target.

HACKING-07.title: Every hack's depth and detection are recorded
HACKING-07.summary: Each intrusion records how deep it went, from a local device up to command systems, and whether the hacker was noticed. That record is what raises Trace, so bigger, noisier hacks draw more Glitterite attention.

HACKING-08.title: What the player sees about hacking
HACKING-08.summary: The player can read a hack's progress, the target's security tier, why a hack is refused, what the remote relay can reach, and a history of past intrusions.

ANDROIDS-01.title: Building androids as full colonists
ANDROIDS-01.summary: At Ultra the colony can manufacture androids that join at once as full colonists able to hold a faith. The ending's argument relies on building them carrying no penalty.

ANDROIDS-02.title: Android-building unlocked by studying Glitterites
ANDROIDS-02.summary: The research that allows building androids requires having studied a captured Glitterite exemplar, optionally plus an Intel-bought techprint. Intel is never charged per android.

ANDROIDS-03.title: Can androids have psychic powers?
ANDROIDS-03.summary: As shipped, no android can hold a psylink. This decides whether they can: all of them, chosen ones, awakened ones, on a story condition, or none.

ANDROIDS-04.title: Psychic rules per kind of android
ANDROIDS-04.summary: Psylink rules can differ for factory-built, arrived, awakened, jailbroken and Glitterite androids. Glitterites stay deaf in every version; out of the box only awakened androids are told apart from the rest.

ANDROIDS-05.title: Captured Glitterites stay prisoners only
ANDROIDS-05.summary: A captured Glitterite holds no faith and can only be held or sold; it is never recruited, enslaved or converted. The prisoner tab reads 'Non-recruitable'.

ANDROIDS-06.title: Jailbreaking a Glitterite into a colonist
ANDROIDS-06.summary: The one exception: an operation on a captured Glitterite gives back its persona and free will, and it becomes an ordinary android colonist. Its price is a persona subcore.

ANDROIDS-07.title: No awakened androids before the Ultra era
ANDROIDS-07.summary: VRE – Android lets outlanders, pirates and the Church field awakened androids 2% of the time from game start. The campaign stops any arriving before Ultra, so nothing shows up above its era.

RESEARCH-01.title: Research unlocked by studying a trophy
RESEARCH-01.summary: A project can require a specific object, like a Glitterite heart or a marauder's sword, brought home and studied at a bench on the player's order. The object survives and can gate several projects.

RESEARCH-02.title: Research unlocked by techprints and instruction
RESEARCH-02.summary: Some projects need Instruction: a techprint or authored item, from a quest or bought with Intel. The largest late projects need Instruction the colony got by trading Intel.

RESEARCH-03.title: Research that uses up materials
RESEARCH-03.summary: Practice: a project costs resources like cloth or leather, spent in trials the player orders, each with its own failure letter. Most routes take the cost before research starts.

RESEARCH-04.title: Dismantling Glitterite artifacts for Intel
RESEARCH-04.summary: The player can order a Glitterite artifact slowly taken apart. Over many sessions it pays Intel and raises Trace, then is destroyed. Unlike studying a surviving exemplar, it never adds research progress.

RESEARCH-05.title: No shortcuts past eras or study gates
RESEARCH-05.summary: Mod features and items that grant research free (a psycast, the schematic book, senator favours, spy thefts) are shut off, so nothing jumps an era or skips a study requirement. It must be in before world creation.

RESEARCH-06.title: Research unlocks basic jobs like mining
RESEARCH-06.summary: In the Neolithic, work such as mining, farming or hunting starts greyed out, naming its project, and goes live the moment it is researched, making 'we learned to mine' a story beat.

ERA-01.title: Advancing the world to the next era
ERA-01.summary: Finishing an era's capstone moves the whole world up one tech era in one step, never automatically and never halfway. The world's tech level and the colony's move together, so the players own the campaign's pacing.

ERA-02.title: Only the capstone can change the era
ERA-02.summary: No mod button, setting or event shifts the era sideways. World Tech Level's in-game 'change tech level' button is removed, so the advance stays the players' act and both players' games agree.

ERA-03.title: A permanent record of when each era began
ERA-03.summary: The game remembers the day every era started, past eras included, so beats can fire e.g. '180 days after the Medieval gate'. It must work when each player's colony runs its own clock (Async Time).

ERA-04.title: Seeing the current era and its start
ERA-04.summary: The planet tab shows which era the world is in, the day it began, and a log of every boundary crossed, so players can read where the campaign stands.

ERA-05.title: Clearing high-tech ruins from the home map
ERA-05.summary: A Neolithic colony should not start beside ancient Ultra-tech dangers, a crashed mechanitor walker, or ancient car wrecks. These are kept off the colony's own map when it is generated.

ERA-06.title: High-tech events wait for their era
ERA-06.summary: Events that belong to a later era, chiefly the crashed mechanitor ship that opens Biotech's mech line, happen in their own era (Industrial) instead of from day one.

ERA-07.title: Swapping out-of-era ruins for era-fitting ones
ERA-07.summary: Instead of just deleting above-era content, put something era-appropriate in its place: a fixture in the yard, or a site a short journey away that becomes part of the campaign's quest line.

ERA-08.title: Nothing arrives from above the current era
ERA-08.summary: Raids, visitors, traders, quests and faction-less events never bring anything from a higher era. Lower-tech arrivals are fine. No faction is exempt, the Empire/Church included; only a deliberately authored beat may break the rule.

ERA-09.title: No drop pods before the Industrial era
ERA-09.summary: Pods belong to Industrial, when the player gets them. Before then, quest rewards, joiners, called aid and siege supplies must arrive some other way than falling from the sky.

ERA-10.title: Every faction's pawns and gear written by us
ERA-10.summary: Every faction, including ones quests and mods create mid-game, fields only the pawn types, gear and xenotypes we wrote, so no in-era faction turns up with a stray high-tech pawn from some mod's additions.

CHARTING-01.title: Finding sites by working an observatory
CHARTING-01.summary: A colonist works a star-reading apparatus to discover sites; nothing is found without that work. It feeds an everyday-sites pool and a story pool, each with a guaranteed eventual find. Skill finds more, not better; idle time is not banked.

CHARTING-02.title: Main-story discoveries arrive in order
CHARTING-02.summary: The Archon storyline's discoveries (the spine) come strictly one after another: the next appears only once the current one is completed. Losing a site keeps that beat's place, and a beat already in play is not handed out twice.

CHARTING-03.title: Everyday optional sites found by surveying
CHARTING-03.summary: Alongside the story, the apparatus turns up ordinary optional sites at about vanilla's rate. Any vanilla or mod quest can be added to this pool.

CHARTING-04.title: Quests announce themselves in later eras
CHARTING-04.summary: Some quests must be charted in early eras but, as the eras advance, show up as ordinary storyteller offers instead. One era test both takes a quest out of the survey pool and lets the storyteller offer it.

CHARTING-05.title: Only finding places you can reach
CHARTING-05.summary: Each era offers search-distance bands and each apparatus accepts a range, so discoveries land only where the colony can actually travel. Better mobility opens farther bands. Within a band, placement is uniform, not biased toward near.

CHARTING-06.title: Star Table, Observatory, Sensory Array tiers
CHARTING-06.summary: The discovery apparatus climbs a ladder of buildings across the eras, each reaching farther, with room for more tiers. A plain 'mundane table' that finds only everyday sites is the same shape.

CHARTING-07.title: Showing discovery progress without spoiling it
CHARTING-07.summary: Players see progress for both searches but no time estimate. The Waystone hints that something is out there the instrument cannot resolve, and each find's letter says why it arrived.

CHARTING-08.title: Caravans and outposts stumble on sites
CHARTING-08.summary: Travelling caravans and scout outposts occasionally turn up ordinary sites next to themselves, with a timer so re-crossing a tile doesn't re-roll. These are everyday finds, never story beats.

CHARTING-09.title: Readable lore found inside sites
CHARTING-09.summary: Sites can hold murals or records a colonist reads if the players care to. Reading pays Intel once, leaves a 'read' version of the object, and the text stays re-readable from History by both players.

CHARTING-10.title: Does orbit use the same discovery apparatus?
CHARTING-10.summary: Odyssey ships an orbital scanner that finds space sites on its own. The choice is whether Charting's apparatus also covers orbit, the scanner delivers Charting's content, or the two share or stay separate.

INFRA-01.title: An unpaved world where road tiers matter
INFRA-01.summary: The world starts with only dirt paths and tracks, no ancient highways. Each road tier gives a distinct travel speed, so better roads are worth building.

INFRA-02.title: Vehicles fast on roads, crawling off them
INFRA-02.summary: Ground vehicles should race along paved roads and be near-useless cross-country, so roads and vehicles reinforce each other. As shipped, many vehicles move at the same speed on any road tier.

INFRA-03.title: Factions build roads to their neighbours
INFRA-03.summary: After each era advance, every civilization gradually paves routes to its own and allied settlements, visibly growing on the map. A broken alliance pauses a road; capturing an endpoint completes it for the new owner.

INFRA-04.title: Paying for a specific road
INFRA-04.summary: The player funds a named road to be built sooner, farther or at a better tier, recognisably different from a gift, through a channel that fits the era: caravan, messenger, radio or pods.

INFRA-05.title: Paying for a better road than planned
INFRA-05.summary: Funding can lift a route above the tier its builder would have laid, e.g. stone instead of dirt, but never above the current era's best.

INFRA-06.title: Colonists pave roads themselves
INFRA-06.summary: Besides funding others' roads, the colony can send its own workers out to build roads directly.

INFRA-07.title: Cars, trucks and aircraft from Industrial
INFRA-07.summary: At Industrial, vehicles arrive: faster world travel, more carrying capacity and combat platforms, with aircraft as a later, separate step. The reachable world expands sharply.

INFRA-08.title: Enemy and trader factions with vehicles
INFRA-08.summary: Partly: NPC factions use the vehicles their era allows, in armoured raids, base defence or trade caravans. Only from Industrial on, since no earlier vehicles exist anywhere.

INFRA-09.title: Better travel lets discovery reach farther
INFRA-09.summary: As roads and vehicles improve, Charting's search can reach farther bands, since the colony can now get there. Mobility offers the reach; the apparatus tier still caps it.

ORBIT-01.title: Orbit stays hidden until the reveal
ORBIT-01.summary: Partly: before the story reveals space, players can't view orbit, fly there or find sites in it. Odyssey fills orbit at world creation and leaves it open from day one, so we must close it.

ORBIT-02.title: No space quests before the reveal
ORBIT-02.summary: Nothing hands out orbital quests early: the orbital scanner, ancient uplinks hacked on the surface, Vanilla Gravship Expanded's scanner cluster and GravTech's core all stay shut until the reveal.

ORBIT-03.title: Orbit stays silent until you can reach it
ORBIT-03.summary: Orbital traders don't call and hidden Salvagers don't raid until the colony can talk to or reach space. Contact follows capability.

ORBIT-04.title: The one-time moment space opens
ORBIT-04.summary: The reveal is earned in the story, happens once for the whole world, and stays open even if whatever earned it (a scanner, a key item) is later lost.

ORBIT-05.title: Orbit fills with factions at the reveal
ORBIT-05.summary: At the reveal the whole orbital board appears at once: spacer powers, surface factions that went up with the players (names and history intact), and the Glitterite settlements.

ORBIT-06.title: Keeping orbital factions from being deleted
ORBIT-06.summary: World Tech Level can silently delete the too-high-tech orbital factions at world creation, so they must be exempted to exist for the reveal. Whether exempting the Empire breaks the no-exempt-faction rule is still open.

ORBIT-07.title: Space stations that change every visit
ORBIT-07.summary: Orbital strongholds generate as floored, heated, pressurised stations with a different layout each visit, with per-type options such as breach chance, derelict or intact, and hackable doors.

ORBIT-08.title: Quest strongholds with guaranteed objectives
ORBIT-08.summary: A station a quest spawns reliably holds the quest's objective, is defended, and the objective can actually be reached. Supports heists: a named vault item, a boss in the objective room, a raid countdown once inside.

ORBIT-09.title: Leaving, returning to and failing strongholds
ORBIT-09.summary: What happens when players leave a stronghold unfinished or fail it: whether the site vanishes, can be revisited with the objective still there, or comes back later as a fresh attempt.

GRAVSHIP-01.title: Living permanently aboard the gravship
GRAVSHIP-01.summary: In the Spacer act the ship becomes the colony's home, and the planetside base can be retired. Deck space, air, heat, food, power and shields all have to work for a whole crew.

GRAVSHIP-02.title: Founders breathe vacuum; others need suits
GRAVSHIP-02.summary: The two founders survive vacuum unprotected, while everyone else must wear vacsuits outside the hull.

GRAVSHIP-03.title: Space disasters and threats in orbit
GRAVSHIP-03.summary: Orbit blocks most events by default, so an orbital home would go quiet. Events, conditions and threats that make sense in space are allowed back, so life aboard stays eventful.

GRAVSHIP-04.title: Recruits and quests reaching the orbital ship
GRAVSHIP-04.summary: Partly: new people can arrive and join, and quests can be offered, while the colony lives in orbit, but only by pod or shuttle; nobody can ever walk in.

GRAVSHIP-05.title: Visitors and trade while living in orbit
GRAVSHIP-05.summary: Partly: visitors and traders can come to the ship, and the crew can trade at stations, but walking caravans can never cross an orbital map edge.

GRAVSHIP-06.title: Ship's destination changes owner mid-flight
GRAVSHIP-06.summary: If the tile a gravship is flying to changes hands in flight, for example an ally takes it, the ship shouldn't blindly land and attack the new owner. The player's choice at launch is respected.

GRAVSHIP-07.title: Ship defenses that climb the eras
GRAVSHIP-07.summary: The hull mounts a defense ladder across the eras: burst shields, turrets, point defense that shoots down pods, then Ultra-tech guns.

COLONY-01.title: Add-bill menu shows current-era recipes first
COLONY-01.summary: When you open a bench's add-bill list, this era's recipes come first and older ones recede. It only reorganises the list; it never removes or locks a recipe, and each player may see their own menu.

COLONY-02.title: Pawns relax at what they're passionate about
COLONY-02.summary: A pawn looking for recreation leans toward activities that train a skill it has a passion for, major passions most. It changes what they do for fun, not how often, and boredom still wins over preference.

COLONY-03.title: Recreation for skills no game trains
COLONY-03.summary: Seven of the twelve skills (medicine, for one) have no recreation that trains them, so passion-led fun can't reach them. Reading the matching textbook, or new recreation we add, fills the gap.

DEFAULTS-01.title: Ready-made role gear sets from day one
DEFAULTS-01.summary: Kits such as a Smith or Miner outfit are authored by us and already exist in a fresh colony, so the player assigns a role's gear rather than building each set by hand.

DEFAULTS-02.title: Gear sets include the weapon
DEFAULTS-02.summary: A kit covers everything the pawn carries, weapon included, not just its clothes and armour. Vanilla outfit policies can't hold a weapon, which is what makes this hard.

DEFAULTS-03.title: Assign a kit once; the pawn dresses itself
DEFAULTS-03.summary: One click hands a pawn its kit, and from then on it keeps itself equipped to that kit, re-gearing on its own after losses or upgrades. Only a custom system gets both halves.

DEFAULTS-04.title: Force a re-gear or strip a pawn
DEFAULTS-04.summary: The player can order a pawn to re-equip its kit now, and to drop what it carries. Vanilla has no 'drop everything' order and won't strip a healthy colonist.

DEFAULTS-05.title: Kits can name gear not yet invented
DEFAULTS-05.summary: A kit may list gear from a later era, such as plate armour in the Neolithic. That's intended: the pawn wears the best it can currently get, and nothing breaks or complains.

DEFAULTS-06.title: New bills open with sensible settings
DEFAULTS-06.summary: A new crafting bill starts pre-set per recipe, e.g. 'do until you have 5, Good quality or better, minimum durability'. It's applied once at creation and never overrides later edits. Reclaim, smelting and butchering bills can't use it.

DEFAULTS-07.title: Copy one bill's settings onto another
DEFAULTS-07.summary: Set up the chest-armour bill once, then paste its count, quality and other settings onto the gloves, helmet and boots bills. The recipe and chosen material are never copied.

ITEMS-01.title: Break down old gear into its material
ITEMS-01.summary: Obsolete apparel, armour and weapons can be reclaimed at a bench for the material they were made from (leather back as leather, steel plate as steel), with no intermediate scrap resource.

ITEMS-02.title: Reclaiming returns half the material
ITEMS-02.summary: Reclaiming gives back 50% of what the item was made of. The engine only allows quarter steps, so 25/50/75/100% are the only possible yields.

ITEMS-03.title: Yield ignores condition and quality
ITEMS-03.summary: A tattered or awful item returns the same share as a pristine one. The player picks which items to feed using the bill's usual durability and quality sliders.

ITEMS-04.title: Reclaiming available from the Neolithic on
ITEMS-04.summary: Reclaiming works in whatever era the colony is in, starting at the tribal crafting spot on day one, optionally with its own dedicated bench.

ITEMS-05.title: Relics and advanced parts are never reclaimed
ITEMS-05.summary: Sanctified relics can't be broken down, and reclaiming never hands back components, chemfuel, subcores or mech resources. Vanilla already enforces both.

ITEMS-06.title: Player can see the reclaim yield
ITEMS-06.summary: Before feeding an item in, the player can learn what fraction comes back. It can only be shown as text in the recipe description, not as a number on the info card.

ITEMS-07.title: Reclaim bills support 'do until you have X'
ITEMS-07.summary: A reclaim bill can run until the stockpile holds a target amount of the material, rather than only Forever or Repeat N. Vanilla can't count these products, so it needs a small piece of code.

SPECIALISATION-01.title: Skilled pawns choose a specialty within a skill
SPECIALISATION-01.summary: As a pawn's skill climbs, the player periodically picks a specialisation inside it (a smith toward weapons, a cook toward gourmet). No new skills or XP; it rides the existing skill.

SPECIALISATION-02.title: Only major passions can specialise
SPECIALISATION-02.summary: A pawn may only specialise in a skill it has a major (double-flame) passion for. Passion can still shift mid-game via genes or growth moments, opening or closing the door.

SPECIALISATION-03.title: Specialisations are small stat bonuses only
SPECIALISATION-03.summary: Each advance is a modest number, typically a 1–5% boost to one stat, and never unlocks new recipes, buildings or other content.

SPECIALISATION-04.title: Smiths split into weaponsmith or armoursmith
SPECIALISATION-04.summary: A smith can lean toward weapons or armour. Vanilla can't tell the two apart (both use the same work-speed stat), so this needs new stats on the recipes or custom code.

SPECIALISATION-05.title: Recruits and captives arrive already specialised
SPECIALISATION-05.summary: Generated pawns such as captives, arrivals and quest pawns come with specialisations fitting their skills, making them prizes or disappointments. The player's starting colonists begin with none.

SPECIALISATION-06.title: Fallback: named specialist posts, one holder each
SPECIALISATION-06.summary: If full specialisation proves too costly, a small fixed set of Ideology-style specialist roles (e.g. weaponsmith) each held by one pawn at a time. Tied to the player faith; not a progression.

SPECIALISATION-07.title: Specialisations are visible and costly to change
SPECIALISATION-07.summary: A pawn's specialty shows plainly (a role, or a 'trained as weaponsmith' health entry) and changing an earned one has a cost, such as a ritual or surgery. Only stated for the post and trained-condition routes.

QUESTS-01.title: Main story is one permanent parent quest
QUESTS-01.summary: The Chronicle shows as a single always-accepted quest that never expires, with each required story beat nested under it in order and a progress count like 3 / 9.

QUESTS-02.title: Each subplot gets its own parent quest
QUESTS-02.summary: Every subplot appears as its own standing quest with its steps nested beneath, no matter how a step arrived: bought in a shop, offered normally or found by Charting.

QUESTS-03.title: Missed story beats come back, never soft-lock
QUESTS-03.summary: Declining, failing or losing a beat (say, its site expires) never breaks the plot line. Only success advances it, so the same beat simply comes round again.

QUESTS-04.title: Plot progress and completed beats stay visible
QUESTS-04.summary: The player can see how far along a plot line is, and finished beats remain readable under their parent. Vanilla drops finished beats flat into the Historical tab, so full legibility needs a small build.

QUESTS-05.title: Every quest shows a difficulty rating
QUESTS-05.summary: Each quest displays its challenge stars before the player commits. About 60 quests across installed mods declare none, and an unrated quest wrongly shows as one star.

QUESTS-06.title: Quest letters say why it's happening
QUESTS-06.summary: Every quest's arrival letter explains its cause in plain words, e.g. 'the Sensory Array caught…', or names the faction leader who is asking.

QUESTS-07.title: Unannounced quests are found through Charting
QUESTS-07.summary: Quests nothing would naturally announce must be discovered by Charting work instead of arriving by letter. As eras advance, some charted quests switch to announcing themselves.

QUESTS-08.title: Required story content never left to chance
QUESTS-08.summary: Anything the campaign needs arrives on a fixed order or guaranteed timer, never on a random roll. Spending elsewhere may slow the Schism plot but can never strand it.

QUESTS-09.title: Quests from storyteller, world map or scheduled events
QUESTS-09.summary: Three ways content reaches the player: the storyteller's random quest pool, something on the world map (the Charting apparatus, caravan finds), or a named event fired on a set day or condition.

QUESTS-10.title: Quests handed over by traders, books or scans
QUESTS-10.summary: Content can be given by a person or thing: a trader, a book being read, an orbital scan, or (only via beggars) a visitor. Givers can be random friendly factions or a named leader.

QUESTS-11.title: Church decrees the colony must fulfil
QUESTS-11.summary: Once the founders hold standing in an institution like the Church, it imposes obligations. Failing one costs mood, Exaltation or goodwill, and decrees stop once the Church turns hostile.

QUESTS-12.title: Quest shops paid in Influence or Intel
QUESTS-12.summary: Missions can be bought in a shop: the Schism's, paid in Influence, or the Glitterite exchange, paid in Intel.

QUESTS-13.title: Shop stock with its own conditions and expiry
QUESTS-13.summary: Each shop entry is a mission or an item (such as a techprint) from an authored list. Each appears when its conditions are met, stays for its own shelf life, and can leave when it no longer qualifies.

QUESTS-14.title: A failed bought mission can return
QUESTS-14.summary: Failing a purchased mission never stalls its plot line. It can come back to the shop free or at full price, or the payment can be refunded, set per entry.

QUESTS-15.title: Both players share one quest board
QUESTS-15.summary: In Multiplayer, both players see and act on the same quest list, as vanilla already works. No build needed, though nothing arbitrates if they disagree.

ALTAR-01.A.plain: Already built into the altar; nothing to do. Charge never decays, and the prisoner-or-slave rule decides who dies.

ALTAR-02.A.plain: A sacrifice rite where the priest kills the qualifying believer. Small build; the game records the death as an executed colonist.

ALTAR-02.B.plain: The believer takes their own life as the rite completes, reusing VIE Memes' ceremonial suicide outcome or a copy. Equally small build.

ALTAR-03.A.plain: Already built: facilities scale the cost with a 25% floor. Their lottery effects (category lean, extra options) do nothing until the lottery exists.

ALTAR-04.A.plain: Already built: the rite grants the named gene and the recipient lives. Which genes exist, and mark-locking them, are still open.

ALTAR-05.A.plain: Our own offer window with no close button, holding the recipient until the player picks. Needs one two-player test to confirm it syncs.

ALTAR-05.B.plain: Fallback only if that test fails: rebuild the offer on Multiplayer's own choice-window pattern, adding a dependency on its API.

ALTAR-06.A.plain: Category printed on the capsule and altar, all four options shown, odds kept hidden. Near-trivial build.

ALTAR-06.B.plain: Also print each option's odds, borrowing another mod's calculation. A little more code; trades mystery for legibility.

ALTAR-07.A.plain: The capsule-less rite grants the gene, records transcendence and opens the Administrator. Fuel refusal checks the founder record, since archons carry the gene.

REVERENCE-01.A.plain: Catch converts and freed believers as they leave the map; quests pay Reverence as a chosen reward. Hard: new saved state and several patches.

REVERENCE-01.C.plain: Optional extra: a data table of which game events move Reverence, and by how much. Pilgrims still need an authored quest.

REVERENCE-02.A.plain: Decay in small capped steps on a neglect timer, like natural goodwill drift; bands defined as data, with a letter per crossing.

REVERENCE-03.D1.plain: A Reverence strip on each row of the vanilla Factions tab. Familiar place, but three mods contest that row; recheck every update.

REVERENCE-03.Own-political-tab.plain: A new tab of our own for Reverence and politics. No conflicts or update upkeep, but a whole screen to design.

REVERENCE-03.D2.plain: Greyed comms-console options that state the Reverence required and the current value.

REVERENCE-04.A.plain: Scale every goodwill change at the single point all pass through; data picks which reasons count. Covers every source, but some previews show unscaled numbers.

REVERENCE-04.A2.plain: As A, plus the difference shows as its own named line ("the government fears your faith"). Explains itself; two messages per change.

REVERENCE-04.B.plain: Scale vanilla's own adjustment step. Previews stay accurate for free, but it cannot tell reasons apart, so every change counts.

REVERENCE-04.C.plain: Scale only chosen sources, one by one. Previews match payouts exactly, but anything unlisted is untouched, and breadth makes it heavy.

REVERENCE-04.D.plain: Reverence shifts the faction's natural goodwill baseline. Only nudges drift; cannot shrink a gain or accelerate one sharply.

REVERENCE-04.E.plain: Cap goodwill while the faction fears the faith, instead of damping gains. A different fiction: no reduction, no acceleration.

REVERENCE-05.A.plain: Institutions live as records on the faction's Reverence entry, founded from a comms option. No world-map presence.

REVERENCE-05.B.plain: Institutions as visible, selectable, caravan-reachable things on settlements. Not recommended: duplicates the number and breaks as settlements come and go.

REVERENCE-05.A+display-adapter.plain: A's record plus a light settlement marker pointing at it, for a world-map presence. Only if a visible marker is wanted.

CHURCH-01.A.plain: Change names, text, creed and look only; keep every internal identifier. Cheap data work, required whatever ceremony is chosen.

CHURCH-01.Ceremony-A.plain: Vanilla's bestowing ceremony reskinned: a Church bestower and honour guard arrive, title psylinks switched off. Free and already a ritual.

CHURCH-01.B.plain: The founders hold their own title ritual and no bestower comes. More work; chosen on fiction alone, e.g. no shuttle for a Medieval Church.

CHURCH-02.A.plain: Relabel vanilla permits and add new ones as data. Title-gated trade already works natively.

CHURCH-03.A.plain: Our own credit choice written into each authored deed: any reward mix, consequences per option. Reaches only quests we write.

CHURCH-03.B.plain: Patch the random reward generator so founder and Schism credit appears on every random-reward quest, other mods' included. Options stay random.

CHURCH-03.C.plain: Vanilla as shipped: Church quests randomly offer Exaltation or other rewards. No founder or Schism credit, so it misses the requirement.

CHURCH-04.A.plain: Write each Church decree's failure cost into its own quest. Easy data work, plus one tiny helper if VFE Deserters is absent.

CHURCH-04.B.plain: One patch: no new decrees while the Church is hostile, and running ones end when it turns.

CHURCH-04.C.plain: A single code hook costing any decree. Not recommended: no other mod issues decrees, so there is nothing to generalise over.

CHURCH-04.D.plain: The Church itself issues decrees on a schedule, not only through a titled colonist's mental break.

CHURCH-05.A.plain: Anyone, as vanilla ships. No work; every titled colonist then gets decrees, permits and trade access.

CHURCH-05.B.plain: Block favour and titles where they are written, refusing or redirecting to a founder. Watertight, but menus still offer everyone.

CHURCH-05.C.plain: Adjust each place the game offers a pawn: accept menu, choose-pawn letter, inheritance, tribute collector. Honest UI, but only those surfaces.

CHURCH-05.D.plain: Restrict by some other test (role, trait, xenotype, seniority) using B's or C's hooks.

CHURCH-05.E.plain: Authored Church deeds name the founder who receives the favour. Covers only quests we write.

CHURCH-06.A.plain: One saved flag capping Church goodwill at -100, so it turns hostile with vanilla's letter and stays hostile. Small code.

CHURCH-06.B.plain: Use VFE Deserters' own permanent-hostility switch, if that mod ships. Nothing to build.

CHURCH-07.U1.plain: The offer itself: a repeating quest shaped like Royal Ascent, gated on the top title; vanilla's Royal Ascent removed. Easy data.

CHURCH-07.A.plain: Accept with a titled founder on a map; a game-over dialog then ends it for both in one click. Needs a two-player test.

CHURCH-07.B.plain: Accept from anywhere, caravans included, with the dialog synced through Multiplayer's API. A rejoining player never sees it.

CHURCH-07.C.plain: Accept from anywhere; each player leaves on their own click. Multiplayer-safe, but the host leaving closes the other's session.

CHURCH-07.D.plain: Accepting starts the ending, and a later act on the map (a shuttle, a rite) finishes it. Changes the requirement's wording.

FOUNDERS-01.A.plain: All seats visible from day one, locked with a stated reason until their milestone. Shows the future; spec recommends.

FOUNDERS-01.B.plain: A seat appears only when its milestone arrives, as a revelation. No hint beforehand and no announcement by default.

FOUNDERS-01.C.plain: The milestone makes a seat available at the next ideology reform; the player decides when or whether. Needs a fluid ideology.

FOUNDERS-02.A.plain: A campaign meme that forces precepts and limits each issue to an allowed set. Easy, survives reforms, fully visible to the player.

FOUNDERS-02.B.plain: A campaign player faction that hides disallowed precepts at creation. Nearly free, but reform, Classic and loading all silently bypass it.

FOUNDERS-02.C.plain: A named campaign faith preset on the ideology page. Carries memes only; everything else is rolled.

FOUNDERS-02.D.plain: Skip the preset page, seed the base, then open the editor for the player to finish, as VFE Tribals does. Delivers it end to end.

FOUNDERS-02.E.plain: Re-apply the base every time the player leaves the ideology page, however the faith was made. A later reform can still undo it.

FOUNDERS-02.F.plain: Gate every precept add at the one check the editor, reform and generator share. Closes B's holes; the floor can move later.

FOUNDERS-02.G.plain: The player hand-installs a campaign ideology file. Not recommended: a mod cannot ship it, and it bypasses every rule.

FOUNDERS-03.A1.plain: Stamp a permanent founder marker on the two starting founders. Survives gene changes, conversion and faction changes; the recommended identity.

FOUNDERS-03.A2.plain: Founders as a special pawn type, usable to pick one in quest data. Breaks when they join the faction or go wild; selector only.

FOUNDERS-03.A3.plain: Identify founders by their genes. Not recommended: converts share them and an implant strips them.

FOUNDERS-03.B1.plain: The quest's accept gate names a founder who must be at the colony; can demand both.

FOUNDERS-03.B2.plain: The player picks which founder accepts the quest, and it is recorded. One founder only; attendance not enforced.

FOUNDERS-03.B3.plain: The quest shuttle lists founders as required and will not leave without them. Easy, but shuttles exist only in later eras.

FOUNDERS-03.B4.plain: The quest checks a founder is present when the caravan reaches the site. Works before shuttles; sees only the first arrival.

FOUNDERS-03.C1.plain: Our own flows, such as revolt contributions, never list a founder. Easy once founders are identified.

FOUNDERS-03.C2.plain: Quest shuttles refuse to load a founder unless required, which also closes vanilla colonist lending.

FOUNDERS-03.C3.plain: An arrested or enslaved founder cannot be sold or gifted.

FOUNDERS-03.D1+D2.plain: Refuse banishing founders outright, or allow banishment but remove the 80% chance a downed founder is left to die for good.

FOUNDERS-03.R1.plain: A founder whose faction has flipped cannot be released as a prisoner to that faction.

FOUNDERS-03.K1..K5.plain: Raiders never choose founders, demands never name them, a kidnapped founder stays the player's with a way home, or raids kidnap nobody.

FOUNDERS-03.C4.plain: Block the faction change at the end of a sale. Not recommended: it fires after the trade, so it fails silently.

FOUNDERS-03.K6.plain: Block the final kidnap step. Not recommended: the founder ends up nowhere, lost without an error.

SCHISM-01.A.plain: Only the faction's official faith changes; existing members keep theirs and newcomers mostly follow. Lightest.

SCHISM-01.B.plain: The official faith and every existing member convert at once.

SCHISM-01.C.plain: A chosen share converts and both faiths coexist. The only route that expresses a partial conversion.

SCHISM-01.D.plain: Rewrite the faction's faith in place. Not recommended: yields a copy, not the Church's own faith, and rewrites every other holder.

SCHISM-02.A.plain: Start: offered as a quest naming a settlement; accept, travel, fight or deliver. Expiry built in.

SCHISM-02.B.plain: Start: a Reverence-gated option in the comms console. Easy once the gated-option display exists.

SCHISM-02.C.plain: Start: in the field, a caravan at the government's settlement triggers it.

SCHISM-02.D.plain: Decider: a friendly faction's forces assault the government beside the player; they cannot be commanded.

SCHISM-02.E.plain: Decider: rebels join the player for the quest, can be drafted, then leave. Gives both players pawns to command.

SCHISM-02.F.plain: Decider: part of the settlement's own garrison switches sides when the player arrives.

SCHISM-02.G.plain: Decider: delivering goods, Influence or pawns; the amount drives success. Can resolve off-map.

SCHISM-02.O1.plain: Outcome: only the faction's faith changes, to the player faith.

SCHISM-02.O2.plain: Outcome: the government is replaced by a new leader and hostility resets; the faction stays independent.

SCHISM-02.O3.plain: Outcome: the faction becomes an ally, temporarily or locked for good.

SCHISM-02.O4.plain: Outcome: some or all of its settlements pass to another existing faction.

SCHISM-02.O5.plain: Outcome: the won settlement becomes the player's, as a home or outpost.

SCHISM-02.O6.plain: Outcome: the faction becomes the player's vassal.

SCHISM-02.O7.plain: Outcome: the rebels split off as a new faction. Forbidden by the requirement.

SCHISM-03.A.plain: A separate Schism faction takes over, and the old Church stays as the hostile remnant. Smaller build; spec recommends.

SCHISM-03.B.plain: The Church faction itself becomes the allied Schism, keeping all Church machinery; a third faction becomes the remnant. Hard.

SCHISM-03.C.plain: VFE Deserters as shipped. Not recommended: never reveals the Schism or moves ground, and its finale ends the game.

SCHISM-03.H1.plain: Vanilla ally stickiness: drift will not break it, attacks will. Free, but fails against faiths with hostile memes.

SCHISM-03.H2.plain: A goodwill modifier keeping the Schism's drift baseline positive whatever the faith differences. Attacks still break it.

SCHISM-03.H3.plain: A stored flag forcing ally status whatever goodwill does. Letting attacks break it needs extra work.

PSYCHIC-01.A.plain: Put vanilla's anima-tree linking ritual on the altar. Needs a meditation focus the recipient can use. Easy data.

PSYCHIC-02.A.plain: Do not ship Vanilla Psycasts Expanded. No XP loop, but the talent tree and founder paths go with it.

PSYCHIC-02.B.plain: Set VPE's XP setting to zero. Easy, but misses three abilities and any player can change it.

PSYCHIC-02.D1.plain: A code gate zeroing all psycast XP; talent points then come only from altar ranks.

PSYCHIC-02.D2.plain: XP still levels a pawn, but only up to a ceiling the altar sets. Keeps meditation as cultivation; spec recommends.

PSYCHIC-02.D3.plain: XP buys psycasts and upgrades, never rank. Changes VPE's economy the most.

PSYCHIC-03.C.plain: Shut each source where it is defined: inert neuroformers, no anima-tree linking, and so on. Mostly data; three need code.

PSYCHIC-03.E.plain: One code gate refusing any rank change not made by the altar. Catches unknown sources but fails silently; backstop only.

PSYCHIC-04.I1.plain: Remove generated psycasters from the world entirely. Easy data; archons still carry innate psylinks.

PSYCHIC-04.I2.plain: Reset rank when a caster joins the player. Enemies keep their powers; captured ones lose them.

PSYCHIC-05.F1.plain: Founders get a special meditation focus from their founder marker, and the path requires it. Strongest key; every leak closes in data.

PSYCHIC-05.F2.plain: The path requires a gene the altar installs. Opens at a story beat, but genes copy and leak; not recommended.

PSYCHIC-05.F3.plain: Use the shipped Transcendent path, keyed on the final rite's gene. Postgame tier only.

PSYCHIC-05.F4a+F4b.plain: Leave VPE's Archotechist path to Church-born pawns, or re-key it for the founders, taking the Church's only native path.

PSYCHIC-05.F5.plain: The path checks the founder marker directly, with no proxy focus in the UI. Medium code.

PSYCHIC-05.F6.plain: Founders get an authored backstory the path requires. No code, but founders' backstories become fixed, and character editors can leak it.

PSYCHIC-06.A.plain: Church caster pawn types with fixed starting levels, independent of titles. Easy data; which types is undecided.

PSYCHIC-07.A.plain: The name appears in the health-tab tooltip only; the row still reads "level N". Easy, partial.

PSYCHIC-07.B.plain: The psylink row itself reads "Psylink (Adept)", always matching the current level.

PSYCHIC-07.E.plain: A real title ladder on a non-Church faction, shown in the Bio tab. Hidden while a Church title is held; the player can renounce it.

PSYCHIC-07.F.plain: The rank as an epithet after the name ("Aria, Adept"). On a founder it shares that slot with the claimed title.

TRANSCENDENCE-01.A.plain: A hidden founder-only health condition holds the record, stamped at game start. Medium code.

TRANSCENDENCE-02.A.plain: A rename-style dialog opened from the founder or the altar. Whether a claim can be retyped is undecided.

TRANSCENDENCE-03.A.plain: Vanilla's per-pawn title field: inspect pane, Bio tab and generated text. No work; absent from the colonist bar.

TRANSCENDENCE-03.N.plain: The claim becomes the founder's nickname: shows on bar and map, but replaces their name in every letter and log.

TRANSCENDENCE-03.C.plain: A display-only tweak putting the claim on the bar and map label, founders only. Long titles get cut off.

TRANSCENDENCE-03.Cprime.plain: Draws a second line or tooltip under the portrait, so a long title shows whole.

TRANSCENDENCE-03.R.plain: A royal title awarded by the player's own faction, beside the Church title. Bio tab only; each founder needs their own title definition.

TRANSCENDENCE-04.A.plain: A vanilla-style dialogue shown to both players; Stay closes it with no effect. Medium code.

TRANSCENDENCE-05.A.plain: Credits roll, then play continues. Leaves the second founder's arc open.

TRANSCENDENCE-05.B.plain: Credits, then each player exits separately. The host skipping first cuts off the other's credits.

TRANSCENDENCE-05.C.plain: Vanilla's game-over dialog; one click ends it for both. Needs a two-player test.

TRANSCENDENCE-05.Cprime.plain: As C, but the exit is delayed a moment for multiplayer safety. Fallback if C's test fails.

POLITICS-01.A.plain: Seed designed alliances and rivalries once at game start, then hook the offending acts; a Vanilla Expanded letter names each knock-on. Seeded ties never drift.

POLITICS-02.A.plain: Copy vanilla's trade-request quest, which already has the countdown and alert; vanilla's goodwill step moves the rival too. Nothing to code.

POLITICS-03.A.plain: The free asks: silver, a delivery to a named tile, or a lent colonist, all from existing vanilla quest pieces.

POLITICS-03.B.plain: Accepting needs a colonist with a given skill, e.g. Medicine 10; the quest shows the requirement until someone qualifies. New code.

POLITICS-03.C.plain: The colony must stop trading with a rival. Needs a small hook to notice trades, since vanilla reports none.

POLITICS-03.L0.plain: Vanilla's colonist loan: shuttle collects, drop pod returns. Only Industrial-or-later askers; pays at hand-over and scores all-dead as success.

POLITICS-03.L1.plain: Pre-pod loan: a caravan walks the specialist to the asker's settlement and hands them over; they walk home when the term ends.

POLITICS-03.L2.plain: Pre-pod loan with no hand-over: the specialist leaves home off-screen and walks back in later. Least code, thinner fiction.

POLITICS-03.E1.plain: Destroy a bandit camp raiding the asker's caravans, using vanilla's own quest and text.

POLITICS-03.E2.plain: Host the asker's refugees on the colony map until they walk out alive; vanilla Royalty quest.

POLITICS-03.E3.plain: The asker's people ride in the colony's caravan to a named settlement. Needs new code for the delivery.

POLITICS-03.P1.plain: Release the prisoner on the colony map; vanilla's own signals detect it. Nothing to code.

POLITICS-03.P2.plain: Hand the prisoner back in person at their settlement by caravan; needs a patch so they don't arrive factionless.

POLITICS-04.A.plain: Our own refusal step fires on expiry: goodwill changes to any factions, plus an optional follow-up retaliation quest.

POLITICS-04.Consequence-raid.plain: The retaliation raid itself: a fixed-faction raid whose size comes from the campaign's pressure system, not the demand.

POLITICS-04.B.plain: Vanilla Factions Expanded Medieval 2's raid-on-fail step. Not recommended as primary: its raid size escapes the pressure system.

POLITICS-05.A.plain: One quest with two branches on vanilla's choice mechanism, built by a small node of ours. A branch without a reward may come up empty.

POLITICS-06.A.plain: A cap counting pending demand offers, with the number set in data. Doesn't restrain demands issued through Vanilla Expanded quest chains.

POLITICS-07.A.plain: A quest offer arrives locked, its requirement box reading 'need N, currently M'; it can't be accepted until met.

POLITICS-07.B.plain: A greyed option on the comms console naming the threshold and current value. Needs a console, so not in early eras.

POLITICS-07.C.plain: A ritual button greyed, with the reason shown, until the standing is reached.

POLITICS-07.D.plain: A building greyed in the Architect menu until the standing is reached; needs a patch to the build menu.

RK-1.plain: Known only while standing stays above a threshold. Nothing stored, so a faction that stops trusting the colony stops confiding. Only standing reveals.

RK-2.plain: Once a faction's feuds are revealed, by standing, quest, comms, battle or letter, they stay known for good.

RK-3.plain: Records single pairs, so a quest or battle can reveal one feud ('the Clans hate the Reach') without the whole list.

RD-1.plain: The Factions tab's 'Enemy of' strip shows only earned enemies; unearned ones are simply absent.

RD-2.plain: An unearned row reads 'Enemies: unknown — revealed at +40', showing the carrot before it's reached.

RD-3.plain: Alliances shown beside enemies on the Factions tab, which vanilla never does. Meaningful only once alliances are seeded.

RD-4.plain: Known enemies and allies listed as a line in the faction's info card.

RD-5.plain: Ask a faction on the comms console who its enemies are; greyed until earned. Unavailable before a console exists.

RD-7.plain: A diplomatic ledger tab of our own listing every known relationship, sortable, with jump-to.

RD-8.plain: Remove the enemy strip entirely; feuds are learned only from letters, quests and dialogue.

RD-6.plain: A letter at the moment of reveal ('the Reach have told us whom they hate'), kept in the history archive.

POLITICS-09.A.plain: A guaranteed meeting whenever a caravan comes into range, with a per-settlement cooldown. Misses parked caravans; vehicle caravans need an extra patch.

POLITICS-09.B.plain: The storyteller rolls encounters near settlements, frequency set per biome. Catches parked and vehicle caravans; quiet caravans slip past more; no guarantee.

POLITICS-09.C.plain: The Faction Territories mod as shipped. Not recommended: declined as a dependency, and it breaks in multiplayer.

POLITICS-10.P1.plain: Vanilla's gifts and peace talks as they ship. The player can't choose who offers talks, and partial payment shows no visible easing.

POLITICS-10.P2.plain: The colony asks a named faction for peace terms; success restores goodwill and ends the declared war.

POLITICS-10.O1.plain: Reparations as a demand: silver, goods, a prisoner, colonists, or a ceded holding; paying it writes the peace.

POLITICS-10.S1.plain: Tribute on a schedule; one missed installment reopens the war the same day. The one substantial build here.

POLITICS-10.B1.plain: A tributary's standing obligations: the overlord asks for levies, a loaned specialist, an embargo, or attendance at its battles.

POLITICS-10.R.plain: Vanilla ransom: buy back kidnapped colonists. No goodwill change and no peace.

POLITICS-10.U1.plain: RimPacts' war score, surrender and tribute treaties. Not recommended: no multiplayer support.

POLITICS-11.E1.plain: A bought truce: fewer or no raids for a window while they stay hostile. The only route while they remain permanent enemies.

POLITICS-11.L.plain: Lift their permanent-enemy status, for good or mid-campaign as a story beat, so normal peace routes apply. Reverses a deliberate design.

TERRITORY-01.Build-B.plain: A timed marker over the ally's own settlement with a 'Join fight' option, so the settlement itself is at stake. Hardest route.

AS-1.plain: An auto-accepted quest places an ally-owned battle site near the ally; attend for a three-way fight, or a roll reports the result.

AS-2.plain: As AS-1, but offered with a response window first; letting it expire reaches the same roll.

AS-3.plain: Worksites Expanded's defend-an-ally beat as the carrier. Hard: it picks its own attacker, rolls unseeded, and isn't authorable.

AS-4.plain: Keep the battle map alive with no player so the NPCs genuinely fight it out unobserved. Not recommended.

OC-C1.plain: A fixed materials-and-silver price per outpost type, carried by the founding caravan. Data only; can't scale by era.

OC-C2.plain: The price rises with the era, or with each outpost already held, softly limiting how many.

OC-C3.plain: Found now and pay later from home; no yield until the debt is paid, which also models build time.

OC-N3.plain: A hard maximum number of outposts, fixed or by era. Only if one is ever wanted.

OC-Y1.plain: Retune yields in data, for the 7 of 13 outpost types that allow it.

OC-Y2.plain: Code the yields for the rest, such as scavenging and town outposts, which ignore data settings.

OC-Y3.plain: Yield depends on who was sent: a slave, prisoner or colonist weighted differently.

OR-1.plain: Staff stay at the outpost, but every recall and management control is removed. They still age, sicken and can die.

OR-2.plain: Ghost staff, but frozen: no aging, disease or death, so the yield stays fixed at what was sent. Cheapest faithful option.

OR-3.plain: Pawns are really sold and gone; the outpost yields a flat amount whoever went. Sending better people earns nothing.

OR-4.plain: Pawns are sold, but a record of their count, skills and kinds sets the yield. Rewards sending better people; more patching.

OR-5.plain: Our own map-less outpost that never holds pawns: a sale at founding, a clock, deliveries. Cleanest for multiplayer, hardest to build.

OU-A2.plain: A quest spawns a hostile camp near the outpost with a deadline; break it or the outpost falls. The fight happens nearby, not there.

OU-A1+OU-A3.plain: A timed attack at the outpost itself, attended or resolved in the colony's absence. Hard; shares the ally-battle machinery.

OU-N1+OU-N2.plain: Non-attack upkeep: a notice letter with an immediate effect, or a declinable quest with a deadline and a refusal consequence.

OU-D1..D4.plain: Softer stakes: a late payout, yield stalled until answered, or, only if staff are kept, a pack-up ultimatum or sick staff needing medicine.

OU-T1..T3.plain: Different events, odds and consequences for each outpost type.

OU-A4.plain: The outpost's own staff fight an ambush on a map. Not recommended: the player can't decline it.

RU-1.plain: The outpost itself is flagged ruined: production stops, goods stay, its label changes; a caravan option rebuilds it.

RU-2.plain: A dedicated ruin on the world map holding the surviving goods, with Loot and Rebuild options for a visiting caravan.

RU-3.plain: The goods lie on a real map the caravan walks, optionally guarded; the site vanishes once left, looted or not.
